rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening question expresses amazement and humiliation at the Quraysh's worship of female-named deities.
rows.anchor: The question posed in these verses is meant to express amazement and humiliation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage invokes Gabriel's obedience and honor before God, alongside power, stature, and wisdom, to frame the rebuke of Quraysh's feminine naming of angels.
rows.anchor: held in honour before the Lord of the Throne, (81:20))

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh are rebuked because Gabriel has lofty masculine attributes while they name deities after women and regard them as God's daughters.
rows.anchor: how can these angels having such lofty manly attributes be compared to their deities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three deities are symbols of angels, as becomes clear from the succeeding verses.
rows.anchor: all three of them are symbols of the angels.

rows.speaker: idolaters of Arabia
rows.claim: Arabian idolaters believed angels were God's daughters and that God did what they asked; they expected the deities to secure worldly provision and children and spare worshippers punishment.
rows.anchor: the idolaters of Arabia regarded the angels to be daughters of God and thought that God did whatever they said.

rows.speaker: idolaters of Arabia
rows.claim: They especially revered Lāt, ʿUzzā, and Manāt and regarded their recommendation and intercession as certain to succeed.
rows.anchor: these three deities had a great status for them. Their recommendation and intercession was considered to bear certain results.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Specific tribes may have been especially attached to one deity, but all Arabian idolaters recognized the three deities' exalted status.
rows.anchor: all the idolaters of Arabia equally acknowledged their exaltedness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh gathered the deities' statues at the Kaʿbah to project political and religious leadership over Arabia; they revered these three most because their worshippers were especially numerous.
rows.anchor: In order to express and impose their political and religious leadership over the whole of Arabia

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deities had graded ranks: Lāt and ʿUzzā were highest, while Manāt, though exalted, ranked below them.
rows.anchor: Lāt and ‘Uzzā had the highest status. Though Manāt was also regarded as very exalted yet it was lower in rank to the other two.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic qualifiers for Manāt indicate its place among the leading deities and its lower relative rank; the words express rank in Arabic, as in 7:39.
rows.anchor: known in Arabic to express rank and status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many exegetical discussions of the names' etymology and meanings are baseless.
rows.anchor: the discussions found in books of exegesis regarding the etymology and meaning of these names is baseless.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Lāt is a distorted form of al-Ālihah, a name adopted for the greatest deity and shortened through common repeated use.
rows.anchor: is a distorted form of

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some derive al-Lāt from a root meaning to dissolve and knead and claim it was a pilgrim-feeder later worshipped at his grave; Islahi rejects this etymology and story.
rows.anchor: Some people regard it from the root

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pilgrim-feeder story contradicts the Qur'an: these were statues of deities formed by naming angels after women.
rows.anchor: they were statues of deities and they were carved out by naming the angels after women.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿUzzā is a feminine form of ʿAzīz/Aʿazza, a prominent divine attribute expressing exaltedness and reverence; the deity is named from this aspect.
rows.anchor: obviously is the feminine form of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manāt derives from maniyya: a deity approached with hope and cherished, or regarded as a means of granting wishes.
rows.anchor: which would mean a deity coming close to which is greatly cherished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentences are sarcastic: Arabs prefer sons and despise daughters, even hiding in embarrassment when a girl is born.
rows.anchor: the Arabs like male offspring and hate female offspring to the extent that whenever a girl is born to them they start hiding themselves from others out of embarrassment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because they dislike daughters for themselves, they should not attribute them to God; assigning Him daughters and themselves sons is an absolutely unfair division.
rows.anchor: What justice can be seen in this distribution for God has created all but they associate daughters to Him and sons to their own selves?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ḍayz means an unjust, unfair thing; the verb ḍāzahu means to oppress or wrong someone.
rows.anchor: means “something which is unjust and unfair.” The verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ascribing either sons or daughters to God violates His oneness as well as human nature and intellect.
rows.anchor: ascribing sons or daughters to God is in the first place totally against God’s oneness as well as human nature and intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their further injustice is to assign God what they find embarrassing for themselves, implicitly treating Him as inferior to them.
rows.anchor: they regard God to be even inferior in status to themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deities are invented names given by the people and their forefathers, with no real beings corresponding to them.
rows.anchor: they are merely names which they and their forefathers have given them and they do not represent any one in the real world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deities have no divine sanction; ancestral practice proves nothing because those ancestors also worshipped by blindly following their forebears.
rows.anchor: If they have found their forefathers worshipping them, then this is not reason enough.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A valid sanction could come from human nature and intellect, God's signs in the outer and inner worlds, or direct communication through prophets and messengers; no such sanction exists here.
rows.anchor: God’s sanction in this regard could have been found in human nature and intellect or could have been found in God’s signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had God endorsed these deities, He could have named them beloved daughters whose intercession He always accepts and whose worshippers He forgives, but He did not.
rows.anchor: He could have said that such and such are his favourite daughters whose recommendation He always accepts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from direct to indirect address rebukes the people's deprivation and intellectual decline: God specially revealed guidance, yet they followed conjecture and whim.
rows.anchor: Here the discourse has become indirect. This is a rebuke on their deprivation and misfortune

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hudā refers to the guidance God revealed in the Qur'an and Sunnah, whose purity and exaltedness the sūrah's opening verses described.
rows.anchor: guidance which the Almighty has revealed in the form of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following conjecture is dangerous generally, and especially reckless when divine guidance is present, like leaping into death in broad daylight.
rows.anchor: following them in spite of the presence of divine guidance is like throwing one self into the pit of death in broad daylight.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about what souls desire specifically refers to the people's polytheistic religious innovation.
rows.anchor: specifically refer to the innovation of polytheism of these people which is under discussion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every religious innovation arises from personal whim; when someone cannot meet reality's demands or easily deny reality, innovation offers an apparent escape from its obligations.
rows.anchor: every innovation originates from some personal whim or wish.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With no intellectual or scriptural evidence, Satan deceived idolaters that angels were God's favored daughters, that He honored their intercession, and that worship would secure worldly goods and a high afterlife status while averting accountability.
rows.anchor: Satan tried to deceive these Idolaters by saying that angels were daughters of God and that such and such daughters were especially dear to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mythology served personal desire: it promised God's nearness and Paradise without requiring people to sacrifice what they wanted.
rows.anchor: what else is the reason behind this mythology other than personal desire and fancy?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about attaining desires expresses amazement at, and comments on, the preceding argument: wishes do not determine what reality grants.
rows.anchor: This is an expression of amazement on what is said above as well as a comment on it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When reality arrives, false hopes collapse: deities cannot help, and each person is judged by deeds, entering Paradise or Hell according to whether good or evil deeds prevail.
rows.anchor: none of their deities will be able to help them in any way; each person will be faced with his deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning applies to everyone: Arabs, Jews, Christians, and Muslims also harbor desires invented by fancy; Islahi connects Jewish and Christian amāniyyu to al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān and says Muslims invented beliefs against Qur'an and Sunnah by following them.
rows.anchor: the Jews, Christians and Muslims too had a lot of desires in their hearts which were a product of their fancy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's general word “man” addresses every individual without exception: desires neither change reality nor make God's law biased.
rows.anchor: By using the general word “man” in this verse, the Qur’ān has addressed each and every individual without any exception

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anyone expecting God's laws to accommodate personal wishes must know that both worlds belong to God; nobody can intercede or change His laws and decisions without His permission.
rows.anchor: both this world and the next are in the complete control of God; no one has the status or stature to intercede before Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse further explains divine control: angels of every rank in heaven cannot intercede without God's permission, and may do so only for someone He permits.
rows.anchor: there are many angels, both of high and low rank, present in the heavens whose intercession will be of no avail to anyone except if God permits them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who invented this angel mythology are those who do not believe in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: they are the ones who do not have faith in the Hereafter
